prompt: On iOS, which folder of the container may the system purge when the disk is nearly full?

choices.text: Documents/
choices.why: Documents holds what the person made, and the system leaves it alone.

choices.text: Library/Application Support/
choices.why: That is where a database the app needs goes, and it is kept.

choices.text: Library/Caches/
choices.why: Right. Caches holds what can be fetched again, and the system may empty it under pressure.

choices.text: Library/Preferences/
choices.why: UserDefaults writes there, and it survives.

prompt: The planner downloads a cover picture for each course from the server. Where should it keep the pictures on Android?

choices.text: In cache/
choices.why: Right. They can be fetched again, so losing them costs one request each.

choices.text: In databases/, beside the sessions, so everything is in one place
choices.why: One place is not the goal; the pictures would then count against the backup like the sessions do.

choices.text: In files/, because the app made them
choices.why: The app did not make them; it downloaded them, and files/ goes into the backup.

choices.text: In shared_prefs/, encoded as text
choices.why: Preferences are for small settings; a picture there is read on every launch.

prompt: Match each Android folder to what belongs in it.

pairs.right: a handful of settings, as XML
a picture that can be downloaded again
an identifier for this one device

right_distractors: a file another app may read

prompt: A React Native app writes a file to Expo's cache directory. Where is it on an iPhone?

choices.text: In a folder React Native keeps outside the app's container, shared by the Expo apps on the phone
choices.why: There is no shared folder: every app has its own container, and the library names a folder inside it.

choices.text: In tmp/
choices.why: tmp/ exists too, but the cache directory is a different folder.

choices.text: In Documents/, since JavaScript cannot see Library/
choices.why: The library reaches Library/ through native code; the cache is there.

choices.text: In Library/Caches/, as for a Swift app
choices.why: Right. The app runs on iOS, so its files land where iOS puts them.

prompt: Why does the course have you run `node show.ts` with no build step?

choices.text: Node 22 compiles TypeScript and checks the types first
choices.why: It checks nothing; it strips the types and runs what is left.

choices.text: Node 22 removes the type annotations and runs the rest
choices.why: Right, and that is also why it does not check the types.

choices.text: better-sqlite3 includes a TypeScript compiler
choices.why: It is a database library and has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: The files are plain JavaScript renamed

prompt: What does the `-E` in `npm install -E better-sqlite3@13.0.3` change in `package.json`?

choices.text: It marks the package as a development dependency
choices.why: That is -D. The package appears under dependencies.

choices.text: It installs the package for each user of the computer
choices.why: That would be a global install, and -E is not one.

choices.text: It makes the download faster and changes no file
choices.why: It changes the line npm writes.

choices.text: It writes 13.0.3 rather than a range such as ^13.0.3
choices.why: Right. The transcript shows "better-sqlite3": "13.0.3" with no caret.

prompt: A student on Windows installs Node.js for Windows from nodejs.org and also has Node in WSL. The course's transcripts show v22.22.0 and theirs show another version. What does the lesson tell them to do?

choices.text: Keep one Node, in WSL's ~/.local/node, and check `which node`
choices.why: Right. Two copies make the version depend on which the terminal finds first.

choices.text: Run the course in PowerShell, where the Windows copy lives
choices.why: Every command is typed in WSL; the lesson says so for Windows.

choices.text: Install a third copy from Ubuntu's packages to break the tie
choices.why: A third copy makes it worse: which one runs depends on the PATH.

choices.text: Ignore it: another version of Node prints the same output
choices.why: Versions differ in what they print and what they run; that is why the course pins one.

prompt: Why is a session's date a string such as 2026-10-21 rather than a timestamp?

choices.text: Strings take less space than numbers in SQLite
choices.why: Space is not the reason, and a number would be smaller.

choices.text: TypeScript has no date type
choices.why: JavaScript has Date; the choice is about meaning, not about the language.

choices.text: It names a day on the calendar, and an instant would shift with the zone
choices.why: Right. Somebody three hours west would see it on the day before.

choices.text: The server cannot read timestamps
choices.why: Every server can; a timestamp would simply say the wrong thing here.

prompt: Using the planner's data, how many minutes are planned in the week that starts on Monday 2026-10-26?
Why does `show.ts` take the week as an argument instead of reading today's date?

choices.text: So it prints the same lines on any day
choices.why: Right. A transcript that depended on today would be wrong tomorrow.

choices.text: Reading the clock is slow
choices.why: It is instant; speed is not the point.

choices.text: Node cannot read the clock
choices.why: It can; new Date() does.

choices.text: Because the data has no dates in it, so the week must come from somewhere else
choices.why: Every session has a date; the week is chosen, not missing.

prompt: An Android app keeps 27 MB that Auto Backup would include. What reaches the person's Google Drive?

choices.text: The first 25 MB, in alphabetical order
choices.why: There is no partial backup; that is the trap the lesson measures.

choices.text: All 27 MB, charged to the person's storage
choices.why: That is closer to iOS, which has no quota per app.

choices.text: None of it
choices.why: Right. Past the 25 MB quota the backup is not made at all.

choices.text: The database, because Android backs up databases first
choices.why: There is no priority; the whole backup is skipped.

prompt: In the lesson's run, how many megabytes did the Android backup come to once files/attachments/ was left out? Answer with two decimal places.
An iOS planner keeps a 24 MB PDF in Documents/ that it can download again. Nothing fails. What does the lesson say is wrong?

choices.text: iOS deletes Documents/ when the disk is full
choices.why: It purges Library/Caches/ and tmp/, not Documents/.

choices.text: The person pays iCloud storage for a file the app could fetch again
choices.why: Right. iOS has no per-app quota, so the cost is silent and it is theirs.

choices.text: The backup stops at 25 MB, as on Android
choices.why: The quota is Android's; iOS took all 27.01 MB.

choices.text: It is fine; a PDF belongs in Documents/
choices.why: A document the person made does. One the app downloaded and can download again does not need backing up.

prompt: On iOS, a single file is left out of backup by setting ___ on its URL.
`node check.ts` fails with `Cannot find package 'better-sqlite3'`, and the path in the message is `/home/ana/elsewhere/check.ts`. What is the cause?

choices.text: better-sqlite3 has no build for that computer
choices.why: That would fail during npm install, not when the program imports it.

choices.text: Node 22 cannot import packages from .ts files
choices.why: check.ts imports it fine from ~/planner.

choices.text: The `type` line is missing from package.json, so Node refuses the import
choices.why: A missing type gives a warning and the program still runs.

choices.text: The program is outside the folder with node_modules
choices.why: Right. Node looks beside the program and in the folders above it.

prompt: Put in order what Node does when check.ts says `import Database from "better-sqlite3"` and `package.json` has no `type` line.
items: tries to read the file as CommonJS
finds import syntax it cannot parse that way
reads the file again as an ES module
runs the program and prints the warning
